frames.narration: A shop has 4 teams: sales, shipping, billing and support. Each means something different by customer: a loyalty tier, addresses, a payer, a requester. All read one shared Customer class, 5 files in all.

Sales adds a loyalty tier. The shared class and the sales app are edited, 2 files, but every file that imports the class has its tests run again: 5 files across 5 teams (the 4 teams and the owner of the shared class).

The team draws 4 bounded contexts, each with its own model and a translation layer, joined by a small published language: 13 files. The same loyalty change edits 3 files (model, translation, app) and re-tests only 3 files, all in the Sales team.

A shortcut skips the translation layer: shipping, billing and support import Sales' Customer type. 8 files, but the loyalty change now edits 5 files across 4 teams. The contexts are separate on paper and conformist in the code.

The opposite extreme: one context per entity, 17 files. A loyalty tier now spans the loyalty, customer and order contexts and their translators: 7 files edited and 10 files in 7 teams' areas re-tested.

Over four changes the files edited are: shared model 8, contexts with translation 12, reusing upstream types 12, context per entity 26. Tests run again: 20, 12, 12 and 38. Translation costs more files for a local change and wins when the other teams' tests are the cost.

Inside a context, aggregates decide which rules are strict. One big aggregate enforces all 5 rules in one transaction but a write locks 5 entities. Order with its lines enforces 2 of 5 and leaves 3 eventual. Every entity alone enforces 1 and leaves 4 eventual.
So find the boundaries of meaning first, connect the contexts on purpose and translate at the edge. Then draw each aggregate around the rules that must never break, and no larger.
